label: Tattoo Idioms
description: How a tattoo is actually drawn — the working traditions, each with its own line weight, palette and rules about what goes solid black. Flash sheets and designs, described the way tattooers describe them.

items.name: american-traditional
items.text: American traditional: heavy black outline, flat limited palette of red, yellow and green, solid black shading in whip and pepper, motifs that read across a room
items.text_short: american traditional, bold line, flat palette

items.name: japanese-irezumi
items.text: Japanese irezumi composition: bold subject over stylised wind bars and finger waves, black background smoke, a palette of indigo, vermilion and green

items.name: blackwork-bold
items.text: blackwork: large fields of solid black against untouched skin, negative space doing the drawing, geometric or organic edges cut clean

items.name: fine-line-micro
items.text: fine-line single-needle work, hairline strokes barely thicker than a pen mark, delicate stipple shading, no outline heavier than the detail

items.name: neo-traditional
items.text: neo-traditional: traditional bones with a wider palette and real rendering — varied line weight, jewel tones, decorative framing

items.name: dotwork-stipple
items.text: dotwork: every value built from stippled dots at varying density, no line shading at all, sacred-geometry framing

items.name: script-lettering
items.text: tattoo lettering: flowing script with confident thick-thin contrast, long connecting flourishes, drawn to sit along a limb

items.name: ornamental-geometry
items.text: ornamental geometry: mandala and filigree bands built to wrap a limb, mirrored motifs, fine repeating detail

items.name: watercolor-splash
items.text: watercolor tattoo: loose pigment washes and drips behind a light line drawing, colour deliberately escaping the outline

items.name: chicano-fine-black
items.text: chicano black-and-grey: soft smooth grey wash, photorealistic rendering, filigree and script accents, no colour at all
